summary: Asked to teach His disciples to pray, Jesus gives them a model prayer, a story of a request at midnight, and the promise of the Father’s best gift.
key_insight: The request came from watching Jesus pray. And the teaching ends not with bread but with the Father giving “the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him.” The sleepy neighbor and the earthly father are not pictures of God but contrasts: if even they give, how much more will He.
story: Jesus was praying in a certain place. When He finished, one of His disciples said to Him, “Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples.”

Jesus said to them, “When you pray, say: Our Father in heaven, Hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come.” They were to ask for His will to be done on earth as in heaven, and for bread day by day. They were to pray, “And forgive us our sins, For we also forgive everyone who is indebted to us,” and to ask Him not to lead them into temptation but to deliver them from the evil one.

Then He gave them a story. Suppose one of them went to a friend at midnight and said, “Friend, lend me three loaves; for a friend of mine has come to me on his journey, and I have nothing to set before him.” And suppose the friend answered from inside, “Do not trouble me; the door is now shut, and my children are with me in bed; I cannot rise and give to you.” Jesus said, “I say to you, though he will not rise and give to him because he is his friend, yet because of his persistence he will rise and give him as many as he needs.”

“So I say to you, ask, and it will be given to you; seek, and you will find; knock, and it will be opened to you.” Everyone who asks receives, the one who seeks finds, and the door is opened to the one who knocks.

Then Jesus spoke to them as fathers. If a son asks for bread, will his father give him a stone? If he asks for a fish, will he give him a serpent, or a scorpion when he asks for an egg? “If you then, being evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him!”

scene.label: As John taught
scene.text: John the Baptist’s disciples were known for fasting and prayers (Luke 5:33). A teacher’s followers were probably marked by the prayers he gave them, so the disciple was asking for a prayer that would mark them as Jesus’ own.

scene.label: A guest at midnight
scene.text: Travelers often walked in the cool of the evening and could arrive late. Hospitality was a sacred duty, and a host with nothing to set before a guest shamed his household. Village bread was baked daily, so neighbors would likely know who still had loaves.

scene.label: The shut door
scene.text: A poor family often slept together on mats in a single room, and the door was barred for the night. Getting up meant lifting the bar and waking the children.

scene.label: “Persistence”
scene.text: Luke’s word means shamelessness. Most read it of the bold neighbor who will not stop knocking; some read it of the sleeper, who would not want the shame of failing a guest in his village. Either way, the bread is given.

scene.label: Words not in every manuscript
scene.text: Many of the oldest manuscripts give a shorter prayer here. They begin simply “Father” and do not have “Your will be done On earth as it is in heaven” or “But deliver us from the evil one.” The NKJV includes these words, which match Matthew 6:9–13; many other translations place them in a footnote.

witnesses.luke: Only Luke tells how the disciples came to ask, and it fits his portrait of Jesus at prayer at every turning point (3:21; 6:12; 9:18, 28). Matthew gives a fuller form of the prayer in the Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 6:9–13); Jesus may well have taught it more than once, though some think Matthew placed it within the teaching he gathered there. Where Matthew’s promise ends with the Father giving “good things” (Matthew 7:11), Luke names the gift: the Holy Spirit.

seeing.reveals: Jesus’ own praying drew His disciples to ask how to pray. He shares with them His way of speaking to God as Father and promises that the Father’s best gift is His own Spirit.
seeing.living: Pray with the boldness of the man knocking at midnight, but never as if God were a sleepy neighbor who must be worn down. Keep asking, seeking and knocking as a child does with a father, and ask above all for the Holy Spirit, the gift He has promised.
seeing.ponder: What would change in your prayers if you truly believed your Father is more ready to give than you are to ask?

preaching.big_idea: Ask boldly, because your Father is more ready to give than any friend or father on earth.
outline: A Father who gives the best gift (11–13)
preaching.watch_for: The passage argues from lesser to greater twice: a reluctant friend still gives (v. 8), and sinful fathers still give good gifts (vv. 11–13), so “how much more” the heavenly Father. The neighbor is a contrast to God, not a picture of Him.
